1.title: Sprint Backlog and Sprint Goal
1.text: Welcome to Module 11: Sprint Backlog and Sprint Goal. In Module 7 you saw them created. Now we look at the artifact itself and its commitment. You will learn what the Sprint Backlog is made of, who owns it, what may change in a Sprint and what may not, and why the Sprint Goal stays fixed.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. State the purpose and attributes of the Sprint Backlog. Explain the Sprint Goal as its commitment. Show how the Sprint Backlog can change without endangering the goal. Give two reasons the Sprint Goal does not change. Tell the Sprint Goal from the Product Goal. And spot the traps: a frozen plan, a changing goal, and a goal treated as a list of items.

1.title: Case Check-In: A Smaller Version
1.text: It is day four of Sprint nine at RideLoop. Wei finds that a smaller version of the item, Unlock with a saved card, would still meet the Sprint Goal. That would free room for the item, Fix the slow station map. At the same time, you notice that the board on the wall has not been updated since Monday. As Scrum Master, you wonder who may change what, and what must never change.

1.title: The Sprint Backlog
1.text: The Sprint Backlog has three parts. The Sprint Goal answers why. The items chosen from the Product Backlog answer what. And an actionable plan for delivering the Increment answers how. Together they are the Developers' own plan. So for the exam: the Sprint Backlog is more than a task list. It is the goal, plus the items, plus the plan. The diagram adds that everyone can see the work as it stands, because the plan is updated throughout the Sprint, in enough detail for the Daily Scrum.

1.title: Attributes of the Sprint Backlog
1.text: The learning objective asks for attributes. It is the Developers' own plan, and they update it. It shows the work as it stands, live and visible to everyone. It is updated all through the Sprint as the team learns. It has enough detail for the Developers to inspect progress at the Daily Scrum. It has three parts, the goal, the items and the plan, and together they are the Sprint Backlog. And it is made in Sprint Planning. The earlier edition called it a forecast, and required one process improvement item in it. That is why the RideLoop board, last updated on Monday, is a problem: a live, visible picture cannot be frozen.

1.title: The Sprint Goal
1.text: The Sprint Goal is "the single objective for the Sprint," and it is a commitment by the Developers. It gives flexibility in the exact work, and it creates coherence and focus, so the team works together rather than on separate initiatives. It is created in Sprint Planning, finalized before the event ends, and added to the Sprint Backlog. During the Sprint, the Developers keep it in mind. It is the commitment of the Sprint Backlog, not of the Product Backlog.

1.title: Sprint Goal and Product Goal
1.text: Do not confuse the two goals. The Sprint Goal is the objective of one Sprint. It lives in the Sprint Backlog, and the whole Scrum Team creates it in Sprint Planning. The Product Goal is the team's long-range target. It lives in the Product Backlog, and the Product Owner develops and communicates it. Each Sprint Goal moves the team toward the Product Goal. One is the step; the other is the destination.

1.title: What May and May Not Change
1.text: What may change during a Sprint, and what may not? The plan may change, the detail may change, and the scope may change. The Sprint Goal may not change. Quality may not decrease, and the Sprint length stays fixed. Scope is renegotiated with the Product Owner, and the Developers still decide how the work is done. The simple version: the goal is fixed, and the scope is flexible.

1.title: Who May Change the Sprint Backlog
1.text: Who may change the Sprint Backlog? The Developers own it, and update the plan at any time. The Product Owner negotiates scope with the Developers, but does not add items directly. Stakeholders and managers do not change it; they influence the Product Backlog through the Product Owner. And the Scrum Master helps both sides, but does not change the Sprint Backlog. So Wei and the team may swap in the smaller item, after talking with Maya.

1.title: Negotiating Scope
1.text: How is scope negotiated? This slide goes beyond the Guide with typical examples. The work turns out different from what was expected. The Developers and the Product Owner talk. They may replace an item with a smaller one, split an item, or drop a lower-priority item, as long as the Sprint Goal is still met. What is not allowed: lowering quality, changing the goal, or extending the Sprint.

1.title: Why the Sprint Goal Does Not Change
1.text: The learning objective asks for reasons why the Sprint Goal does not change. These go beyond the Guide. It is a commitment, and changing it would empty the commitment of meaning. It gives focus and coherence. It is a stable target for inspection at the Daily Scrum and the Review. It supports predictability and trust, because stakeholders can rely on what the Sprint is for. The flexibility sits in the scope, so the goal can stay. And if the goal is truly obsolete, the right response is to cancel, not to quietly change it.

1.title: How the Sprint Backlog Is Used
1.text: Follow the Sprint Backlog through the Sprint. In Planning it is created. At the Daily Scrum it is inspected and adapted. All through the Sprint, it is updated as the team learns. At the Review, the Sprint Goal explains what the Sprint aimed at, while the Increment is shown. And at the Retrospective, the most impactful improvements may be added to the next Sprint Backlog.

1.title: Traps: What the Exam Expects
1.text: Here are the traps. The Sprint Backlog is goal, items and plan, not only a task list. The Developers own it, and nobody assigns or adds tasks. It is updated throughout the Sprint, not frozen. The goal is fixed, and scope is negotiated. Quality does not decrease to protect scope. An obsolete goal lets the Product Owner cancel, while being behind does not. And the Sprint Goal is not a list of items: one missed item does not automatically miss the goal.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Recap. The Sprint Backlog is the goal, the items and the plan, and it belongs to the Developers. The Sprint Goal is one objective, and a commitment. The plan and the scope may change; the goal and the quality may not. Scope is negotiated with the Product Owner. The goal stays fixed because it is a commitment that gives focus and a stable target. And the Product Goal is the long-term target above it.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Midway through Sprint nine, Grace asks Maya to add a new, unrelated item to the Sprint Backlog. What should happen? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. The Sprint Backlog is the Developers' plan. New work goes to the Product Backlog, and Maya negotiates with the Developers if it must enter this Sprint, without endangering the Sprint Goal. Nobody else adds items to the Sprint Backlog.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. On day four, Grace wants to change the Sprint Goal to a new priority, although the current goal is still valuable. What is the best answer? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. The Sprint Goal does not change during the Sprint. The new priority is a Product Backlog matter, and only the Product Owner could cancel a Sprint, and only if the goal were obsolete.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. The team treats the Sprint Goal as a list of items, and when one item fails it declares the Sprint a failure. What does the Guide suggest? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. The Sprint Goal is one objective for the Sprint, and it leaves flexibility in the exact work. The Developers and the Product Owner negotiate scope without affecting the goal.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which statement describes the Sprint Backlog? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. It is the Developers' own plan, kept visible and updated all through the Sprint. It is not owned by the Product Owner, it is not frozen, and the long-term list is the Product Backlog.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Which is a reason why the Sprint Goal does not change during the Sprint? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. It is a commitment that gives coherence and focus, and a stable target to inspect against, while the scope stays flexible. It does not guarantee that every item is finished.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: B. New work goes to the Product Backlog, and scope is negotiated. Question two: A. The Sprint Goal does not change. Question three: B. The goal is one objective with flexible work. Question four: A. The Developers' own plan. Question five: D. A commitment, focus, and a stable target. That completes Module 11. Next, Module 12 covers the Increment and the Definition of Done.
